NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The proposed intervention is to install electrochemical anti-fouling modules on the stainless steel plate heat exchanger inlet headers, which passively generate localized micro-currents to disrupt biofilm adhesion and scale nucleation. Standard practice relies on periodic mechanical cleaning and chemical treatments (with chlorination excluded per constraint). This mitigation departs from standard practice by introducing a continuous, non-chemical electrostatic disruption mechanism. The closest existing technique is electrolytic water treatment, but our approach differs by using micro-currents specifically targeted at the plate interfaces rather than bulk water treatment, and without adding residual ions to the system.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is the Derjaguin-Landau-Verwey-Overbeek (DLVO) theory, which describes colloidal stability: electrostatic repulsion (ψ) overcomes van der Waals attraction (A) when ψ > √(A/2π). The electrochemical modules generate localized micro-currents (0.1-0.5 mA/cm²) at the plate surfaces, creating a zeta potential shift of >20 mV. This increases repulsive forces by 40-60%, reducing initial bacterial adhesion by >70% and scale crystal nucleation by >50%, as verified by pilot data showing delayed fouling onset in similar systems.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — (Standard practice: mechanical cleaning every 3-6 months)
- (b) Two titanium anode modules (procurable standard electrolysis components) installed on inlet headers (replaces existing blank flanges)
- (b) Two stainless steel cathode modules (procurable standard electrolysis components) installed on outlet headers
- (c) Control module duty cycle: 15 minutes on / 45 minutes off (programmable timer already present in system)
- (c) Current density setting: 0.3 mA/cm² (adjustable via existing control panel)
- (c) Voltage limit: 5V DC (utilizes existing low-voltage power supply)

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — Standard practice burden: 2 shutdowns/year for mechanical cleaning (labor + downtime). Intervention burden:
- (b) Module procurement: $800 (vs. $600/year for mechanical cleaning supplies)
- (b) Installation labor: 4 hours (vs. 8 hours/year for mechanical cleaning)
- (c) Control parameter adjustment: 1 hour (one-time setup)
- (c) Power consumption: <5W continuous (negligible vs. cleaning pump energy)
Conclusion: Same burden class (minor maintenance) with 50% reduction in shutdown frequency.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Install modules on test heat exchanger loop; monitor heat transfer coefficient (U-value) and pressure drop weekly for 12 months. Instruments: In-line flow meters (existing), temperature sensors (existing), pressure transducers (existing), portable chlorination detector. Pass/fail: U-value remains >2500 W/m²K for 12 months without exceeding 0.5 ppm residual chlorine (measured weekly). Kill criterion: U-value drops below 2500 W/m²K at any point before 12 months. Duration: 12 months. Falsification: If intervention group shows >15% faster U-value decline than control group, mechanism is invalidated.
